lessons.title: What an Exchange Rate Actually Is: Direct and Indirect Quotes, Spot and Forward

children.text: Every time you check USD/INR on Google or an international transfer app, you see a number like 83.42. That single figure hides a convention you need to get right before anything else in this course makes sense: which currency is the price actually measured in, and for delivery when. Get the convention wrong and a straightforward rate reading turns into a costly error, whether you are pricing an export invoice, reading an RBI policy note, or just trying to understand why the business news says the rupee "weakened" today.

body.text: An exchange rate is the price of one currency stated in terms of another. Direct quotes, indirect quotes, spot rates and forward rates are not different things, they are just different ways of expressing or timing that same underlying price.

children.text: Direct and Indirect Quotes: Two Ways to Say the Same Price

markDefs.definition: A quote that states how many units of the domestic currency are needed to buy one unit of a foreign currency. This is the convention India uses for the rupee.

children.text: A
direct quote

states how many units of your home currency it takes to buy one unit of a foreign currency. When you read USD/INR = 83.42, you are reading a direct quote from India's perspective: it takes ₹83.42 to buy $1. This is the convention India uses for every major pair, USD/INR, EUR/INR, GBP/INR and JPY/INR, on NSE, in RBI publications, and on every forex app in the country.

markDefs.definition: A quote that states how many units of a foreign currency one unit of the domestic currency can buy. The mirror image of a direct quote, and simply its reciprocal.

children.text: An
indirect quote

flips this around: it states how many units of a foreign currency one unit of your home currency buys. The same USD/INR relationship, read indirectly from India's side, would be INR/USD = 0.01199, meaning ₹1 buys about $0.01199. It is exactly the same price, just the reciprocal (1 ÷ 83.42 = 0.01199). India almost never quotes rupees this way, but you will run into indirect quotes reading foreign financial press: the UK has historically quoted GBP indirectly against the dollar (GBP/USD, not USD/GBP), and so has the euro area for EUR/USD.

children.text: How India Actually Quotes the Rupee

Every major source you will use in this course, the RBI's daily reference rate, the NSE currency futures order book, or a forex card rate at a bank, quotes USD/INR the same direct way: rupees per dollar. Retail traders access this exact same NSE quote through brokers like Zerodha's Kite platform when they trade USD/INR futures. One consistent convention across policymakers, exchanges and retail platforms means you can compare an RBI statement, an NSE contract price and your bank's forex card rate without doing any conversion in your head.

body.text: Do not assume every country quotes its currency the way India quotes the rupee. If you read "GBP/USD rose to 1.27" in the international press, that is an indirect quote from the UK's point of view: $1.27 buys £1. Flip the logic when you cross from Indian sources into UK or eurozone sources, or you will misread whether a currency actually strengthened or weakened.

children.text: Spot Rate vs. Forward Rate: Same Pair, Different Delivery Date

markDefs.definition: Two business days after the trade date, the standard cycle on which currency and funds are actually exchanged in a spot forex deal.

children.text: The 83.42 you see quoted right now is a
spot rate
, the price for near-immediate delivery. "Near-immediate" in the forex market has a precise meaning: settlement happens on a
T+2 cycle

, meaning the actual currency and rupees change hands two business days after the trade date, not instantly. This is the number that changes every second the market is open, and the one every ticker, app and newspaper headline reports by default.

markDefs.definition: The principle that the forward rate is mathematically pinned down by the interest rate gap between two currencies, not by anyone's guess about future spot prices. Covered in full in Chapter 2.

children.text: A
forward rate

is a price agreed today for delivery on a specific future date, say 90 days from now, regardless of where the spot rate actually ends up on that day. It is easy to assume a forward rate is just the market's forecast of the future spot rate. It is not. A forward rate is arithmetic, derived from the gap between the two countries' interest rates under a rule called
covered interest rate parity

. You will work through that formula in the next chapter. For now, the point to hold onto is simpler: the forward rate for a currency pair is almost never identical to today's spot rate, and the direction of that gap is not random.

columns.label: Spot Rate
points: Price for near-immediate delivery, T+2 settlement
The number quoted on Google, forex apps and NSE tickers by default
Changes constantly while the market is open
What you pay or receive if you convert currency today

columns.label: Forward Rate
points: Price locked in today for delivery on a fixed future date
Used by importers and exporters to hedge currency risk
Set once the deal is struck; does not move with the market afterward
Derived from the interest rate gap between the two currencies, not a prediction

children.text: A Real Example: Pricing a 90-Day Software Export Invoice

A Bengaluru software firm raises an invoice for $50,000, payable by a US client in 90 days. Today's spot USD/INR is ₹83.00. If the firm waits and simply converts whatever it receives in 90 days at whatever the spot rate happens to be then, it is carrying real risk: if the rupee strengthens to ₹81, the firm collects ₹40,50,000 instead of the ₹41,50,000 it expected. Indian interest rates have historically run higher than US interest rates, which under covered interest rate parity means the dollar typically trades at a forward premium against the rupee, so the 90-day forward rate might be quoted at ₹83.90. By booking a forward contract with its bank today, the firm locks in ₹83.90 per dollar regardless of where spot actually lands in 90 days.

body.label: Certainty Gained by Forward Cover
body.context: $50,000 x ₹83.90, locked in today instead of an uncertain amount 90 days from now

body.title: Should the Exporter Hedge?
body.scenario: The same Bengaluru firm's finance head argues against booking the forward: "Our economist thinks the rupee will actually weaken to ₹85 in 90 days, not strengthen. If we are right, hedging at ₹83.90 loses us money compared to just waiting and converting at spot."
body.prompt: Is this a sound reason to skip the forward cover? What is the finance head actually doing when they make this argument, and what is the real purpose of a forward contract for an exporter with a genuine $50,000 receivable?
body.modelAnswer: The finance head is not hedging, they are speculating on a currency forecast, which is a different decision than managing a known receivable. A forward contract's purpose is to remove uncertainty about a real, contracted cash flow, not to maximise the conversion rate. If the firm skips the forward because it expects the rupee to weaken and it is wrong, even by a small margin, it has taken on open currency risk on a $50,000 invoice for no operational reason. The correct comparison is not "forward rate vs. our forecast of spot," it is "known, certain proceeds vs. unknown, variable proceeds." Most treasury policies for genuine trade receivables favour hedging precisely because the firm is in the business of writing software, not forecasting currencies.

body.title: Quick Check
body.question: A UK newspaper reports "GBP/USD fell to 1.24 today, from 1.27 yesterday." What actually happened to the pound?
options: The pound strengthened against the dollar
The pound weakened against the dollar
The dollar weakened against the pound
Cannot be determined without knowing the RBI reference rate
body.explanation: GBP/USD is an indirect quote from the UK's side: it states how many dollars one pound buys. A fall from 1.27 to 1.24 means one pound now buys fewer dollars, so the pound weakened against the dollar. This is the mirror image of how India quotes USD/INR, where a rise in the number means the rupee weakened, so it is worth pausing every time you cross between direct-quote and indirect-quote sources.

points: An exchange rate is simply the price of one currency in terms of another. Direct and indirect quotes, and spot and forward rates, are different ways of expressing or timing that same price, not different things.
India quotes the rupee directly: rupees needed to buy one unit of foreign currency, e.g. USD/INR = 83.42. This convention is consistent across the RBI, NSE and every forex app.
Many foreign sources, including GBP/USD and EUR/USD, quote indirectly from their own currency's side. Always check which convention a source is using before reading a rate move.

A spot rate is the price for near-immediate delivery, settled T+2. A forward rate is a price locked in today for delivery on a specific future date, and is derived from the interest rate gap between two currencies, not a forecast.

Forward contracts exist to remove uncertainty on a known cash flow, not to bet on where a currency will move. The full formula behind forward pricing, covered interest rate parity, is built out in the next chapter.
